Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1133.) The result is called the “lodestar” figure. (Id.)  Other considerations that may result in an upward or downward shift of the fees include the novelty and difficulty of the case, the legal skill needed to render services to the prevailing party, the customary fee for similar work, whether the case was taken under contingency, the attorneys’ experience and reputation, and other circumstances. (Serrano v. Priest (1977) 20 Cal.3d 25, 48-49.)

 

-----

Discussion

 

Plaintiff is the Prevailing Party in this Action & the Attorney’s Fees Provision Applies to this Action –

Here, on October 10, 2025, the parties reached a settlement agreement, whereby GM agreed to pay Plaintiff’s attorney fees, expenses, and costs “that have been reasonably incurred pursuant to California Civil Code § 1794(d) may be determined by the Court via noticed motion. For purposes of any such motion, GM will agree that Plaintiff is the prevailing party.” (Demery Decl., ¶ 10, Exh. 2, ¶¶ 2-3.) GM does not dispute Plaintiff’s status or the application of the provision here. Thus, the Court finds that, per the terms of the settlement agreement, Plaintiff is the prevailing party. In addition, the Court finds that Plaintiff is entitled to an award of reasonable attorney fees pursuant to the settlement agreement.

-----

 

Calculation of the Fee Award – The party seeking fees and costs “bear[s] the burden of establishing entitlement to an award and documenting the appropriate hours expended and hourly rates.” (ComputerXpress, Inc. v. Jackson (2001) 93 Cal.App.4th 993, 1020.) In determining a reasonable attorney fee award, a court decides the “reasonable hours spent” on the case and multiplies the number by “the hourly prevailing rate for private attorneys in the community conducting noncontingent litigation of the same type.” (Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1133.) The result is called the “lodestar” figure. (Id.)

 

Plaintiff’s motion seeks a total of $67,594.87 in fees and costs. Breaking this down, this consists of: (1) $42,640.50 in lodestar fees for 109.8 hours of purported work; (2) a 1.5 times multiplier of $21,320.25; (3); $2,200.00 in “anticipated” fees; and (4) $1,434.12 for costs. (Gruszecki Decl. ¶ 12.)

 

 

i.                Hourly Rate

 

Reasonable attorneys’ fees are determined by examining the time spent and the reasonable hourly rate charged. (Serrano v. Priest (1977) 20 Cal.3d 25, 48-49.) Other considerations that may result in an upward or downward shift of the fees include the novelty and difficulty of the case, the legal skill needed to render services to the prevailing party, the customary fee for similar work, whether the case was taken under contingency, the attorneys’ experience and reputation, and other circumstances. (Id.)

 

Here, Plaintiff seeks to recover a total of $67,594.87 (including a 1.5 times multiplier) in attorney fees, costs, and expenses for work it claims was performed by 7 attorneys: (1) Carey Wood - $560.00/hour; (2) Destinae Demery - $440.00/hour; (3) Vanessa Oliva - $540.00/hour; (4) Iraida Gonzalez - $480.00/hour; (5) Laura Schwartz - $450.00/hour; (6) Shayla White - $430.00/hour; and (7) Bobby C. Walker - $440.00/hour. (Mot., at p. 13.) Plaintiff also seeks to recover for work performed by paralegals at a rate of $215/hour. (Id.) In support of the billing rates, Destinae Demery declared their rates accord with community standards, and the motion cited the finding in Goglin v. BMW of North America (2016) 4 Cal.App.5th 462, 473, affirming that a $575 hourly fee for lead counsel on a lemon law case was reasonable. (Demery Decl., ¶¶ 12-18.)

 

 GM does not challenge the reasonableness of the hourly fee rates.

 

As the rates are not contested, the Court will accept their reasonableness for the purposes of the present motion. This expressly is not an independent determination by the Court of the reasonableness of the rates, and this Order should not be relied on in other litigations as evidence that a court made an independent fiding that the hourly rates listed are reasonable.

 

ii.              Reasonableness of Time Spent

 

GM argues that the following reductions are necessary:

·       Templated Discovery Requests, ESI Letter & PMQ Deposition Notice - 2.7/$1,215.00

·       Templated Discovery Responses - 3.0/$1,350.00

·       Templated Meet and Confer Correspondence 3.6/$1,620.00

·       Templated Motion to Compel the Deposition of GM’s PMQ 12.9/$5,779.00

·       Templated Fee Motion - 1.2/$528.00

·       Pre-Litigation Work - 3.3/$872.00

·       Administrative and Clerical Time - 25.4/$5,461.00

·       Clerical & Administrative Tasks Billed at Attorney Rates - 8.7/$4,278.00

·       TOTAL: 60.8/$21,103.00

 

Total reduction sought in lodestar fees amounts to 60.8 hours, in the amount of $21,103.00 The Court has reviewed the billing records submitted and finds that in some instances the attorneys billed unreasonable hours for certain work,

 

As to GM’s claims regarding the templated discovery requests and responses, meet and confer correspondences, and motions:

 

1.     While the Court does not find the discovery requests work conducted by Laura Schwartz on September 3, 5, and 6 to be excessive, the court does find Laura Schwartz’s and Kenneth Lima’s discovery request entries on September 12 and 13 to be duplicative of previously billed work and reduces the 0.2 hours ($90) spent by Schwartz and the 0.7 hours ($150.50) spent by Lima. (Total: $240.50)

2.     The Court does not find that Counsel excessively billed for the discovery responses on October 17 & 28, and November 12, 2024, because each discovery request was billed for less than an hour.

3.     The Court finds that  counsel unreasonably billed 5.1 hours for meet and confer efforts throughout the months of October and November 2024 considering the relative simplicity and similarity of meet and confer emails. The Court reduces by 3.6 hours ($1,620.00)

4.     The Court finds that counsel unreasonably billed for work as to the motion to compel the deposition of GM’s PMQ. First, Lauren Schwartz excessively billed 2.4 hours for drafting a reply in support of the motion, so the Court reduces the hours by 1.4 ($630.00). Second, the Court finds Kenneth Lima’s billing for reviewing and finalizing the reply to be duplicative of work billed by Lauren Schwartz and reduces the 0.2 hours billed ($43.00). Third, the Court finds Lauren Schwartz’s billing for Review ROA in anticipation of motion to compel PMQ hearing on March 17, 2025, to be duplicative of Lima’s billed work on the same day and reduces the 0.2 hours billed ($90). Fourth, the Court finds Destinae Demery’s billed work for analyzing and reviewing Plaintiff’s MTC PMQ depo to be duplicative of work billed by other attorneys and reduces the 1.8 hours ($792). Lastly, the Court finds Destinae Demery’s 1.8 hours for drafting demand for expert exchange and depo notices and subpoenas on August 14, 2025 to be excessive and reduces by 0.8 hours ($352). (Total: $1,907)

5.     The Court does not find 2.7 hours for auditing billing records and accounting for this motion plus drafting this motion to be excessive. However, the Court finds 5.2 hours for reviewing the opposition and drafting a reply to be excessive and reduces by 3.2 hours ($1,408).

6.     The Court does not find GM’s argument that work related to the case, even if done prior to the complaint being filed, is unrecoverable. However, the Court does find the 0.2 hours billed by Jonathan Avalos on July 11, 2024, for a voicemail and email requesting Plaintiff to call back to be unreasonable as a recoverable cost ($43).

7.     The Court does not find GM’s argument regarding administrative and clerical time billed by paralegals to be persuasive because GM does not provide support or evidence that serving, receipt and reviewing, scheduling, and calendaring are purely clerical tasks rather than tasks usually associated with and conducted by paralegals in support of litigation. GM also argues in broad strokes rather than pinpointing specific entries for the Court. The Court has reduced duplicative hours above for paralegal work.

8.     The Court does not find GM’s argument regarding alleged clerical and administrative tasks billed at attorney rates persuasive, because GM makes general allegations without providing specific evidence or entries supporting its claims. The Court cannot determine which entries GM is referring to due to the lack of information.

 

The Court calculates the total amount of these reductions to be $5,218.5. Subtracting this amount from the fees sought of $44,840.50 ($42,640.50 in incurred fees and $2,200.00 in “anticipated” fees)  amounts to fees of $39,622.

 

GM also requests a 10% reduction of Counsel’s time, or a reduction of $2,153.75, because 15 individuals billed on this matter without an explanation or justification for such a breadth of timekeepers in a common Song-Beverly Act case. (Opp., at p. 11.) Plaintiff does not address this argument in their reply. The Court understands that inefficiencies occur through the use of multiple timekeepers, and the Court has attempted to address some of those inefficiencies above. Fifteen timekeepers for this matter is excessive, however. The Court further reduces the fees by 5% to account for these inefficiencies, and to account for block-billing of entries.. (Morris v. Hyundai Motor America (2019) 41 Cal.App.5th 24, 39.) This results in an additional discount of $1981, for fees of $37,641.

 

GM also requests a reduction of $931.03 in costs on the grounds that the costs were not required, and no jury convened as to the CMC and notice of posting jury fees. However, GM has not filed a motion to strike or to tax costs. (Cal. rule 3.1700(b).) Thus, Plaintiff’s request for costs is not reduced.

 

iii.             Multiplier

 

The Court agrees with GM that a “multiplier” is unjustified here. This was an ordinary lemon law case that did not require extraordinary legal skill, did not get past the earliest stages of discovery, and was resolved in a little over a year since the initial complaint was filed. Plaintiff argues a multiplier is justified because counsel obtained an “excellent” outcome, of the “contingent risk,” the complexity of the case, and counsel’s skill in litigating this matter, but fails to persuasively satisfy the elements required for an enhancement. Thus, under the circumstances, the Court finds a multiplier is not justified.

 

Therefore, Plaintiff is entitled to recover attorney fees in the reduced amount of $37,872, plus $1,434.12 in costs.

 

-----

 

 III.          Conclusion

 

Plaintiff’s Motion for Attorney Fees is GRANTED in the reduced amount of $37,461, plus $1,434.12 in costs.

 


Case Number: 25AVCV00022    Hearing Date: July 7, 2026    Dept: A14

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES – NORTH DISTRICT

 

 

IRENE PENA, individually and as surviving spouse of Decedent RAYMUNDO RIVERA, and MICHELLE RIVERA,

 

Plaintiffs, 

v. 

 

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES, a public entity, LOS ANGELES COUNTY SHERIFF’S DEPARTMENT, a public entity, AARON TANNER, individually and as a Deputy Sheriff, and DOES 1 through 50, inclusive,

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case Number 25AVCV00022

 

  [TENTATIVE] 

  STATEMENT OF DECISION 

 

 

  Date of Hearing: July 7, 2026

  Dept. A-14 

  Judge William H. Forman 

 

 

      I.          Background

 

This is a wrongful death and civil rights action arising from the death of Decedent Raymundo Rivera (Decedent) following a pursuit by deputies of the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department (LASD).

 

On January 8, 2025, Plaintiffs Irene Pena (Pena) and Michelle Rivera (Rivera) (together Plaintiffs) filed their complaint against Defendants County of Los Angeles (County), LASD, (together Defendants), and Aaron Tanner (Tanner).

 

On March 4, 2025, the County and LASD filed a Notice of Removal to Federal Court.

 

On April 25, 2025, the United States District Court for the Central District of California remanded the case to Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles.

 

On May 1, 2025, the Notice of Remand was filed in the present action.

 

On June 13, 2025, Plaintiffs filed a Motion for Leave to file a First Amended Complaint.

 

On July 30, 2025, Defendants filed their Opposition to Plaintiffs’ Motion for Leave.

 

On August 11, 2025, the Court deemed the First Amended Complaint filed as of June 13, 2025. (Minute Order dated August 11, 2025.)

 

On August 27, 2025, Defendants demurred to Plaintiffs’ First Amended Complaint.

 

On September 23, 2025, the Court sustained the Demurrer to the First Amended Complaint with leave to amend.

 

On October 16, 2025, Plaintiffs filed their Second Amended Complaint.

 

On October 29, 2025, Defendants demurred to the Second Amended Complaint.

 

On February 23, 2026, the Court sustained the Demurrer to the Second Amended Complaint with leave to amend.

 

On March 11, 2026, Plaintiffs filed their Third Amended Complaint against Defendants LASD, the County, and Tanner asserting causes of action for (1) wrongful death, (2) negligence, (3) failure to supervise and train, and (4) violation of the Bane Act.

 

Pena is the surviving spouse of Decedent, and Rivera is the adult daughter of Decedent. (TAC, ¶¶ 3-4.) Plaintiffs allege that on August 11, 2018, Decedent fled on foot and was pursued by deputies of LASD, including Defendant Tanner, though the circumstances under which the pursuit arose remain unclear. (TAC, ¶¶ 31-32.) After fleeing on foot, Decedent sought refuge within a hollow pillar at a WinCo supermarket to evade capture by the deputies, which Plaintiffs state was hazardous and confined with no safe means of escape. (TAC, ¶ 32.) Plaintiffs claim the deputies intentionally left Decedent stuck in the pillar despite having the means to rescue him, ultimately leading to his death. (TAC, ¶ 33.) Plaintiffs further contend the deputies falsified official reports which misled investigators and the public, and that Plaintiffs detrimentally relied on said reports, which caused them to believe Decedent’s death was an accident. (TAC, ¶¶ 34-35.) Plaintiffs claim they first became aware of wrongdoing on Defendants’ and Tanner’s part on May 28, 2024 via a lawsuit filed by Tanner’s ex-girlfriend, which detailed the deputies’ misconduct and intentional decision to leave Decedent in the pillar. (TAC, ¶ 35.)

 

On April 1, 2026, Defendants demurred to the Third Amended Complaint (TAC).

 

On June 11, 2026, Plaintiffs filed their Opposition to the Demurrer (Opposition).

 

On June 26, 2026, Defendants filed their Reply.

 

Defendant Tanner has not appeared in the case.

 

-----

 

   II.          Preliminary Procedural Issues

 

Meet and Confer Requirement – Before filing a demurrer, the demurring party is required to meet and confer at least five days before the date the responsive pleading is due, in person, by telephone, or by video conference, with the party who filed the pleading demurred to for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.41, subd. (a).) The demurring party shall file and serve with the demurrer a declaration stating the means by which the parties met and conferred and that the parties did not reach an agreement to resolve the issues raised, or that the party who filed the pleading demurred to failed to respond or otherwise failed to meet and confer in good faith. (Ibid.)

 

Here, Defendants provide the Declaration of Blessing O. Ekpezu (Ekpezu Declaration), counsel for Defendants, for satisfaction of the meet and confer requirement. Ekpezu states that on March 20, 2026, he sent an email to Plaintiffs’ counsel outlining the grounds for Defendants’ intended demurrer to the TAC, but that Plaintiffs’ counsel has not agreed to withdraw the TAC. (Ekpezu Decl., ¶ 3.) Because the parties did not meet and confer in person, by telephone, or by video conference, and because Ekpezu does not state that Plaintiffs did not respond or failed to meet and confer in good faith, the Court finds that the meet and confer requirement has not been satisfied.

 

However, a determination that the meet and confer process was not sufficient is not grounds to overrule a demurrer. (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.41, subd. (a)(4).) Accordingly, the Court will consider the Demurrer on the merits notwithstanding Defendants’ noncompliance.

 

-----

 

 III.          Request for Judicial Notice

 

Defendants’ Request for Judicial Notice – Defendants request the Court take judicial notice of (1) the Court’s February 23, 2026 Minute Order and (2) Plaintiffs’ Third Amended Complaint filed on March 11, 2026.

 

California Evidence Code section 452 permits judicial notice being taken of the records of any court in California. (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (d).) California Evidence Code section 453 mandates a court take judicial notice of a matter specified in section 452 if a party so requests, gives the adverse party sufficient notice through pleadings or otherwise, and furnishes the court with sufficient information to enable it to take judicial notice. (Evid. Code, § 453, subd. (a), (b).)

 

Here, the Court notes a request for judicial notice of the TAC is unnecessary, given the Court must consider and take as true all factual allegations within the TAC to properly rule on Defendants’ Demurrer. Regardless, the Court finds that both documents are records of the California Superior Court, County of Los Angeles, have been sufficiently identified and provided by Defendants, and were served along with the request on Plaintiffs on March 31, 2026, providing sufficient notice through the moving papers.

 

Accordingly, Defendants’ Request for Judicial Notice is GRANTED.

 

-----

 

 IV.          Legal Standard

 

Standard for Demurrer – A party against whom a complaint has been filed may object by demurrer to the pleading on the ground that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. (Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10, subd. (e).) A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) When considering demurrers, courts read the allegations reasonably, liberally, and in context. (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.)

As a general matter, in a demurrer proceeding, the defects must be apparent on the face of the pleading or via proper judicial notice. (Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994.) “A demurrer tests the pleading alone, and not the evidence or facts alleged.” (E-Fab, Inc. v. Accountants, Inc. Servs. (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1308, 1315.) As such, the court assumes the truth of the complaint’s properly pleaded or implied factual allegations. (Ibid.) Courts must “treat the demurrer as admitting all material facts properly pleaded, but not contentions, deductions or conclusions of fact or law.” (Blank, supra, 39 Cal.3d at 318.) The only issue a demurrer is concerned with is whether the complaint, as it stands, states a cause of action. (Hahn, supra, 147 Cal.App.4th at 747.)

"[A]bsent a showing of prejudice to the adverse party, the rule of great liberality in allowing amendment of pleadings will prevail." (Board of Trustees v. Superior Court (2007) 149 Cal.App.4th 1154, 1163.) Thus, where a demurrer is sustained, leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (Goodman v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 348.) The burden is on the plaintiff to show the court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Id.; Lewis v. YouTube, LLC (2015) 244 Cal.App.4th 118, 226.) The threshold for meeting this burden is low, and “[i]f there is any reasonable possibility that the plaintiff can state a good cause of action, it is error to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend.” (Youngman v. Nevada Irrigation Dist. (1969) 70 Cal.2d 240, 245).

 

The liberal policy favoring amendments is not without limitation. In response to a demurrer and prior to the case being at issue, a complaint “shall not be amended more than three times, absent an offer to the trial court as to such additional facts to be pleaded that there is a reasonable possibility the defect can be cured to state a cause of action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.41, subd. (e)(1).) However, the “three-amendment limit shall not include an amendment made without leave of the court pursuant to Section 472, provided the amendment is made before a demurrer to the original complaint or cross-complaint is filed.” (Ibid.) California Code of Civil Procedure section 472, subdivision (a) states that “[a] party may amend its pleading once without leave of the court at any time before the answer, demurrer, or motion to strike is filed, or after a demurrer or motion to strike is filed but before the demurrer or motion to strike is heard if the amended pleading is filed and served no later than the date for filing an opposition to the demurrer or motion to strike.”

 

-----

 

    V.          Discussion

 

Application – Defendants demurrer to the TAC in its entirety and all causes of action asserted therein without leave to amend for failure to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action pursuant to California Code of Civil Procedure section 430.10, subdivision (e) on two grounds: (1) the action is time-barred under Government Code section 945.6, and (2) the action is time-barred based on Plaintiffs’ own allegations establishing inquiry notice of wrongdoing in 2018. (Demurrer, p. 3:6-21.)

 

a.     Time-Barred Pursuant to Government Code Section 945.6

 

Defendants first demurrer on the grounds that this action is judicially time-barred pursuant to Government Code section 945.6. Specifically, Defendants note that the County of Los Angeles rejected Plaintiffs’ government tort claim on June 17, 2026, that Plaintiffs had until December 17, 2024, six months from the date of rejection, to file suit under Section 945.6, and that Plaintiffs’ filing of the Complaint in the present matter on January 8, 2025 was twenty-two days late, rendering the Complaint fatally defective. (Demurrer, p. 5:7-10.)

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs claim Defendants’ arguments have already been established by this Court as a factual dispute unresolvable on demurrer. (Opp., p. 6:24-7:2.) Plaintiffs further acknowledge that Defendants have identified no new judicially noticeable facts eliminating the existence of a factual dispute on the issue and dismissal on demurrer remains improper. (Opp., p.7:7-8.) The Court agrees.

 

Defendants’ Demurrer to the Second Amended Complaint came before the Court on February 18, 2026. On February 23, 2026, the Court issued its ruling on the issue of timeliness pursuant to Government Code section 945.6, in which Defendants’ present arguments were thoroughly addressed.

 

In the Court’s Ruling on the matter, this Court noted, in relevant part:

 

“Under Government Code Section 945.6, the operative date for triggering the six-month period to file is “the date such notice [of rejection of the claim] is personally delivered or deposited in the mail.” [Emphasis added.] While the SAC refers to a “June 17, 2024 rejection of Plaintiffs’ tort claim” there is no allegation as to the date of personal delivery or mailing of the rejection letter. The June 17, 2024 in the RJN does contain a mailing date. But while the Court may take judicial notice of the existence of the June 17, 2024 [letter of rejection], the Court may not take judicial notice of the truth of matters stated in the letter or of disputed adjudicative facts. (Fowler v. Howell (1996) 42 Cal.App.4th 1746, 1749-1750.) Plaintiffs’ counsel confirmed at the hearing on this matter that Plaintiffs dispute the statement in the June 17, 2024 as to the mailing date. The Court realizes that in the end the facts could show that the June 17, 2024 letter was mailed that same day. But as the Complaint does not recite a mailing date, the Court cannot resolve this disputed fact on demurrer. For that reason, the Court is inclined to bifurcate discovery and trial of the statute of limitations defense and set an early trial on that defense.”

 

(Ruling on Submitted Matter dated February 23, 2026.)

 

As previously stated by this Court, the operative date is the date of personal delivery or the date of deposit of the rejection notice in the mail. The Court is not permitted under well-established law to take judicial notice of disputed or disputable factual allegations. Further, Plaintiffs represented that they do dispute this date and no date of mailing was pleaded in any complaint filed by Plaintiffs. Thus, the Court is not permitted now, as it was not in February, to take the June 17, 2024 date as indisputable fact on demurrer, as it is not judicially noticeable.

 

Defendant further argues in reply to Plaintiffs’ argument that in light of the Court’s February 23, 2026 ruling on the issue, Plaintiffs had ample opportunity to plead a mailing date and set forth factual contentions as to this issue in the TAC but failed to do so. (Reply, p. 2:20-25.)

 

Defendant has misread the Court’s prior Order. The Court did not sustain the demurrer as to the issue of Government Code Section 945.6 notice, or require Plaintiff to provide additional allegations as to a mailing date. The February 23rd Order sustaining Defendants’ demurrer to the Second Amended Complaint states, in relevant part, “the Demurrer is SUSTAINED WITH LEAVE TO AMEND regarding Plaintiffs’ allegations supporting the supposed May 2024 accrual date and why and how the claim did not accrue earlier. Leave is not granted as to any other allegation.” (Minute Order dated February 23, 2026 (emphasis added).) Defendants’ argument that Plaintiffs’ failure to include a purported mailing date to raise a disputable issue in the TAC fails on the basis that doing so would be a direct violation of the Court’s Ruling and would constitute noncompliance with the narrow leave granted for amendment of the Second Amended Complaint.

 

Furthermore, the Order limiting discovery to the questions of the mailing date and equitable tolling made clear that the Court regards the mailing date as a critical factual issue that should be resolved early in the litigation. The Court hopes the parties have made progress on this front.

 

Accordingly, Defendants’ Demurrer on the grounds that the action is time-barred under Government Code section 945.6 is OVERRULED.

 

b.     Time-Barred Based on Inquiry Notice

 

Defendants demur on the ground that Plaintiffs were on inquiry notice in 2018 after Decedent’s death pursuant to the discovery rule, and accordingly, the action is time-barred by the statute of limitations. (Demurrer, p. 9:8-26.)

 

Plaintiffs argue in opposition that the facts pleaded in the TAC do not establish inquiry notice as a matter of law, that the TAC adequately alleges fraudulent concealment and equitable estoppel, and that Plaintiffs have alleged facts sufficient to show diligent inquiry and investigation into suspicions, all of which led to a conclusion that Plaintiffs legally had no recourse as no wrongdoing had been uncovered. (Opp., p. 4:244-5:2, 13-22.)

 

Shirk v. Vista Unified Sch. Dist.(2007) 42 Cal. 4th 201, 208-09 describes the necessity of timely claim presentation and the significance of claim accrual: “Accrual of the cause of action for purposes of the government claims statute is the date of accrual that would pertain under the statute of limitations applicable to a dispute between private litigants. [Citations.]” [Internal citations omitted.]

 

Thus, whether a claim is timely presented depends on when the claim accrued, as otherwise provided for in the law. On a demurrer, the complaint must allege timely presentation after accrual:

 

“Complaints that do not allege facts demonstrating either that a claim was timely presented or that compliance with the claims statute is excused are subject to a general demurrer for not stating facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. [Citation.]”

 

(Id., at 209 (internal citations omitted.)

 

Plaintiffs argue they have alleged additional facts in the TAC sufficient to allege a May 2024 accrual date of this action, relying on the discovery rule.

 

“The discovery rule only delays accrual until the plaintiff has, or should have, inquiry notice of the cause of action. The discovery rule does not encourage dilatory tactics because plaintiffs are charged with presumptive knowledge of an injury if they have ‘information of circumstances to put [them] on inquiry’ or if they have ‘the opportunity to obtain knowledge from sources open to [their] investigation.’ [Citations.] In other words, plaintiffs are required to conduct a reasonable investigation after becoming aware of an injury, and are charged with knowledge of the information that would have been revealed by such an investigation.” (Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc. (2005) 35 Cal. 4th 797, 807-808 (internal citations omitted).)

 

“A plaintiff whose complaint shows on its face that his claim would be barred without the benefit of the discovery rule must specifically plead facts to show (1) the time and manner of discovery and (2) the inability to have made earlier discovery despite reasonable diligence." (McKelvey v. Boeing North American, Inc. (1999) 74 Cal.App.4th 151, 160, 86 Cal.Rptr.2d 645.) “In assessing the sufficiency of the allegations of delayed discovery, the court places the burden on the plaintiff to ‘show diligence’; ‘conclusory allegations will not withstand demurrer.’ [Citation.]” (Fox, supra, 35 Cal.4th at 808.)

 

As the Supreme Court held in Fox:

 

“[T]o employ the discovery rule to delay accrual of a cause of action, a potential plaintiff who suspects that an injury has been wrongfully caused must conduct a reasonable investigation of all potential causes of that injury. If such an investigation would have disclosed a factual basis for a cause of action, the statute of limitations begins to run on that cause of action when the investigation would have brought such information to light. In order to adequately allege facts supporting a theory of delayed discovery, the plaintiff must plead that, despite diligent investigation of the circumstances of the injury, he or she could not have reasonably discovered facts supporting the cause of action within the applicable statute of limitations period.”

 

(Id at 808-09.)

 

Thus, Plaintiffs are charged with demonstrating through specific facts that they conducted a reasonable investigation of all potential causes of Decedent’s death or wrongdoing on behalf of Defendants, during and after which they had no reason to suspect, nor reason to discover, facts supporting the present action against Defendants.

 

Here, taking Plaintiffs’ factual assertions in the TAC as true, the Court finds Plaintiffs have not plead additional facts sufficient to support a cause of action with an accrual date of May 28, 2024, and in light of the circumstances alleged, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiffs’ actions and investigation into Decedent’s death were reasonable.

 

Plaintiffs’ TAC states that deputies falsified official reports, which stated Decedent’s death was accidental, and that Plaintiffs relied on these falsified reports and believed the death was accidental. (TAC, ¶¶ 34-35.) The TAC further states that Plaintiffs were not aware that these reports were falsified until May 28, 2024, when Tanner’s ex-girlfriend filed a lawsuit exposing the deputies’ misconduct, including the deliberate decision to leave Decedent trapped and subsequently fabricate reports to conceal their actions. (TAC, ¶ 35.) Plaintiffs further allege they had “no reason to suspect wrongdoing or investigate further.” (TAC, ¶ 19.)

 

Plaintiffs also allege a number of new facts in the TAC related to their belief that Decedent’s death was accidental. Plaintiffs allege that upon Pena’s learning of her husband’s death, she repeatedly contacted the sheriff’s department and investigators to obtain more information regarding the circumstances of his death, but received inconsistent and confusing information. (TAC, ¶ 35(I)-(J).) Pena contacted the coroner and attempted to contact the physician she was told had information regarding Decedent. ((TAC, ¶ 35(L)-(M).) After receiving additional conflicting and concerning information regarding the physician from Detective Fierro with LASD, Pena suspected she was not receiving clear or truthful information regarding Decedent’s death, but states that because all official information provided to Plaintiffs characterized the death as accidental and in the absence of evidence suggesting wrongdoing, Plaintiffs believed the death was an accident. (TAC, ¶ 35(M)-(P).) However, Plaintiffs then allege that Pena attempted to obtain legal representation “to pursue justice for her husband,” consulted with multiple attorneys “regarding the possibility of bringing legal action related to Decedent’s death,” and “spent several months communicating” with an attorney who agreed to further review the matter. (TAC, ¶ 35(Q)-(S).)

 

The factual allegations of Plaintiffs’ TAC are inconsistent, stating both that they had no reason to suspect wrongdoing or investigate, and that Pena suspected she was not receiving truthful information regarding the circumstances of her husband’s death, and after said suspicion arose, consulted with numerous attorneys to review the matter further, determine the existence of a legal cause of action, and get justice for her husband’s death. These additional allegations included in the TAC, taken as true, indicate Plaintiffs were suspicious and on notice of potential wrongdoing or concealed information on behalf of Defendants and that Plaintiffs were questioning the circumstances surrounding Decedent’s death. This suspicion gave rise to a responsibility to conduct a reasonable investigation into all potential causes of death.

 

Plaintiffs fail to plead facts sufficient to show a reasonable investigation. Plaintiffs allege that multiple attorneys declined representation based on the official reports provided by law enforcement, that the attorney who agreed to further review the matter determined that he could not locate a legal basis to pursue a claim, and Plaintiffs concluded no legal action could be pursued “based on the official information provided by law enforcement.” (TAC, ¶ 35(R)-(U) (emphasis added.) In light of any allegation to the contrary, these statements show that Plaintiffs based their conclusion that the death was accidental only on the official information provided by law enforcement, which Pena knew was inconsistent and suspected was false. The TAC also implies the reviewing attorney based his conclusion on the same and provides no further factual information as to investigation of the matter, only stating the attorney reviewed information provided. No facts are alleged as to Plaintiffs’ own investigations, the documents and records requested or uncovered, the witnesses spoken to, or any additional steps taken to investigate the circumstances of Decedent’s death beyond reliance on conflicting official information.

 

Plaintiffs also do not allege that reasonable investigation into the circumstances of Decedent’s death would not have uncovered this information sooner than May of 2024 when Tanner’s ex-girlfriend filed a lawsuit publicizing the wrongdoing.

 

Taking Plaintiffs’ allegations in the TAC as true, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiffs conducted reasonable investigation where they relied on official reports, the veracity of which they questioned, and where no factual allegations indicate that the Plaintiffs lacked the ability to have made an earlier discovery despite reasonable diligence.

 

Accordingly, Defendants’ Demurrer to Plaintiffs’ Third Amended Complaint is SUSTAINED.

 

                                                  i.     Leave to Amend

 

The Court notes that the three-amendment limit in this case does not apply, as Plaintiffs filed their First Amended Complaint before a demurrer to the original complaint was filed and without leave of court pursuant to California Code of Civil Procedure section 472.

 

The Court finds in light of the above circumstances, there is a reasonable possibility of amendment to state an accrual date of May 2024. While the factual assertions within the TAC are contradictory to some extent, these contradictions may possibly be cured in light of additional allegations or factual circumstances, as may Plaintiffs’ failure to plead specific facts related to reasonable investigatory steps taken in light of their suspicions regarding the circumstances surrounding Decedent’s death.

 

In light of the liberal policy of amendment in California, the Court thereby sustains Defendants’ Demurrer with leave to amend regarding Plaintiffs’ allegations supporting the May 2024 accrual date, how and why the claim did not accrue earlier, and steps taken to reasonably investigate as required for their assertion of delayed discovery. Leave to amend is not granted as to any other allegation.

 

-----

 

 

 VI.          Conclusion

 

Defendants County of Los Angeles and Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department’s Demurrer to Plaintiffs’ Third Amended Complaint is SUSTAINED WITH LEAVE TO AMEND.

 

At the hearing on this matter, the Court will discuss whether the question of the mailing date of the June 17, 2024 rejection letter should be set for separate trial.


Case Number: 25AVCV00137    Hearing Date: July 7, 2026    Dept: A14

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES – NORTH DISTRICT

 

 

JOSEPH MILLER,

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

VOLKSWAGEN GROUP OF AMERICA, INC.; AUDI VALENCIA; and DOES 1 though 10, inclusive, 

 

Defendants. 

  Case Number 25AVCV00137

 

  [TENTATIVE] 

  STATEMENT OF DECISION 

 

 

  Date of Hearing: July 7, 2026

  Dept. A-14 

  Judge William H. Forman 

 

 

      I.          Background

 

This is a case regarding violation of statutory obligations under the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act.

 

On January 31, 2025, Plaintiff filed his complaint.

 

On April 18, 2025, Volkswagen filed its demurrer to the complaint.

 

On May 20, 2025, Plaintiff filed his first amended complaint (FAC) against Defendants Volkswagen Group of America, Inc. (Volkswagen) and Audi Valencia (Audi), asserting causes of action for (1) violation of subdivision (d) of Civil Code section 1793.2, (2) violation of subdivision (b) of Civil Code section 1793.2, (3) violation of subdivision (a)(3) of Civil Code section 1793.2, (4) breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, (5) negligent repair, and (6) fraudulent inducement – concealment.

 

Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that on or about March 31, 2022, he entered into a warranty contract with Volkswagen regarding a 2022 Audi E-tron, which was manufactured and distributed by Volkswagen. (FAC, ¶ 10.) Plaintiff avers that defects and nonconformities to warranty manifested themselves within the applicable express warranty period, including electric battery defects, electrical defects, and other nonconformities and defects, which have substantially impaired the use, value, or safety of the vehicle and rendered the vehicle’s value worthless or de minimis. (FAC, ¶¶ 19-21.) Plaintiff claims Volkswagen failed to promptly replace the vehicle or promptly make restitution in accordance with the Song-Beverly Act. (FAC, ¶ 23.)

 

On April 3, 2026, Volkswagen filed its motion to compel the deposition of Plaintiff and request for monetary sanctions.

 

On June 22, 2026, Plaintiff filed a notice of settlement of the entire case. That same day, Plaintiff filed his notice of withdrawal of the notice of settlement of the entire case.

 

No opposition to the motion to compel deposition has been filed.

 

-----

 

   II.          Legal Standard

 

Standard for Motion to Compel Deposition – Any party may obtain discovery, subject to restrictions, by taking the oral deposition of any person, including any party to the action.¿(Code of Civ. Proc., § 2025.010.)¿¿A properly served deposition notice is effective to require a party or party-affiliated deponent to attend and to testify, as well as to produce documents for inspection and copying.¿(Code of Civ. Proc., § 2025.280, subd. (a).)¿¿¿

“If, after service of a deposition notice, a party to the action . . ., without having served a valid objection under Section 2025.410, fails to appear for examination, or to proceed with it, or to produce for inspection any document . . . described in the deposition notice, the party giving notice may move for an order compelling deponent’s attendance and testimony, and the production . . . of any document . . . described in the deposition notice.”¿(Code of Civ. Proc., § 2025.450, subd. (a).)¿¿The motion must set forth facts showing both good cause justifying the demand for any documents and a meet and confer declaration.¿(Code of Civ. Proc., § 2025.450, subds. (b)(1), (b)(2).)

Meet and Confer Requirement – The motion shall be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Section 2016.040, or, when the deponent fails to attend the deposition and produce the documents, electronically stored information, or things described in the deposition notice, by a declaration stating that the petitioner has contacted the deponent to inquire about the nonappearance.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.450 subd. (b)(2).) 

 

-----

 

 III.          Discussion

 

Application – Volkswagen moves to compel Plaintiff’s deposition following his purported refusal to appear for his deposition and the refusal of his counsel to reasonably meet and confer in good faith to schedule the deposition on mutually agreeable dates. (Motion, p. 8-11.) Volkswagen alleges that on March 31, 2025, Volkswagen served Plaintiff with a notice of representation to Plaintiff’s counsel, which informed Plaintiff of its intent to depose Plaintiff within 90 days and requested Plaintiff’s availability to be deposed. (Kim Decl., ¶ 3, Ex. A.) Plaintiff did not respond to this request. (Ibid.)

 

On July 18, 2025, Volkswagen served its notice of deposition, scheduled for September 17, 2025. (Kim Decl., ¶ 4, Ex. B.) Plaintiff served his objection to the notice of deposition on September 15, 2025, stating he was unavailable, that he would meet and confer with Volkswagen to reschedule the deposition on a mutually agreeable date and time, and provided February 2, 2026, as a date of availability. (Ibid.)

 

On October 10, 2025, Volkswagen served its amended notice of deposition scheduled for February 2, 2026. (Kim Decl., ¶ 5, Ex. C.) On January 30, 2026, Plaintiff served an objection to the amended notice of deposition, again stating his unavailability for the scheduled date, stating the parties were meeting and conferring to reschedule the deposition. (Ibid.) Since this objection, Volkswagen has continuously followed up with Plaintiff’s counsel to either settle the case or move forward with discovery, but Plaintiff has failed to respond. (Kim Decl., ¶ 6, Ex. D.)

 

On March 26, 2026, Volkswagen served a meet and confer letter to Plaintiff’s counsel regarding Plaintiff’s deposition, accompanied by a further notice of deposition scheduling Plaintiff’s deposition for April 1, 2026. (Kim Decl., ¶ 7, Ex. D, E.) On April 1, 2026, Plaintiff objected to the amended notice, and since has continued to be unresponsive to Defendant’s efforts to resolve the matter. (Kim Decl., ¶ 8, Ex. F.) Plaintiff has failed to respond to any of Defendant’s efforts to set the deposition, has not provided any alternative dates, and has not responded to offers of settlement. (Kim Decl., ¶ 9.)

 

a.     Meet and Confer Requirement

 

Volkswagen’s counsel, Alexander Y. Kim, submitted his declaration (Kim Declaration), in which he states Volkswagen continuously followed up with Plaintiff after his objection to the latest notice of deposition. Attached as Exhibit D to the Kim Declaration are copies of emails sent by Volkswagen, including an email sent on April 3, 2026, after Plaintiff’s objection.

 

The Court finds that Volkswagen has satisfied the meet and confer requirement.

 

b.     Good Cause

 

Volkswagen has shown good cause for compelling Plaintiff’s deposition. Volkswagen is entitled as a legal matter of right to take Plaintiff’s deposition in this matter. (Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.010.) Volkswagen properly served three separate deposition notices on Plaintiff, which alone is effective to require a party-deponent to attend and to testify. (Cal. Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.240, subd. (a).) Further, Volkswagen has made clear that it seeks Plaintiff’s deposition to gather pertinent information, assess his claims and credibility, and evaluate the extent of his alleged damages which he put at issue in this case. (Motion, p. 7:19-22.) In short, Volkswagen states that its ability to depose Plaintiff is critical to its evaluation of the presented claims and preparing for trial. (Motion, p. 8:8-9.) The Court also notes the trial date of August 28, 2026, and the impending discovery cut-off date of July 29, 2026.

 

While a party may object to a unilaterally scheduled deposition due to unavailability. he may not evade the discovery process entirely by refusing to make himself available or failing to supply alternative dates of availability. Here, Plaintiff objected to three separate deposition notices, including one set for February 2, 2026, a date proposed by Plaintiff. Plaintiff served this objection just three days before the deposition, and months after the deposition was noticed. The Court finds that this objection was not in good faith. Plaintiff has neither met nor conferred with Volkswagen to resolve the issue nor proposed alternate dates of availability. Furthermore, Plaintiff has not objected to this motion to compel to address any reason why the motion should not be granted.

 

Accordingly, Volkswagen’s motion to compel Plaintiff’s deposition is GRANTED.

 

c.      Request for Monetary Sanctions

 

Volkswagen requests monetary sanctions in the amount of $2,567.50. The Court has discretion to impose a monetary sanction on a party who has engaged in the misuse of the discovery process. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2023.030, subd. (a).)

 

Here, Volkswagen’s counsel Kim states that he charges $395 per hour in his representation of Volkswagen. (Kim Decl., ¶ 11.) Kim asserts that he spent at least one hour preparing the deposition notices, meet and confer correspondence, and email correspondences in an effort to take Plaintiff’s deposition, at least two and a half hours preparing the present motion and accompanying declaration, and anticipates an additional three hours of work on this matter to review and analyze the anticipated opposition, prepare a reply, and prepare for and attend hearing on this matter. (Id at 12-14.)

 

The Court notes that no opposition was filed, and as such, no review or reply preparation was required. Otherwise, the Court finds the rate and work done on this matter reasonable. Furthermore, Volkswagen’s request for monetary sanctions remains unopposed.

 

Accordingly, Volkswagen’s request for monetary sanctions for misuse of the discovery process is GRANTED in the amount of $2,000, the amount requested by Volkswagen less $567.50 for approximately one and a half hours anticipated for review of Plaintiff’s opposition and drafting of a reply.

-----

 

 IV.          Conclusion

 

Defendant Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.’s Motion to Compel the Deposition of Plaintiff Joseph Miller is GRANTED. Plaintiff is to appear for deposition within 15 days of this Order.

 

Defendant Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.’s Request for Monetary Sanctions is GRANTED. Plaintiff is ordered to pay to Volkswagen Group of America, Inc. sanctions in the amount of $2,000 within 30 days of this Order.


Case Number: 25AVCV00263    Hearing Date: July 7, 2026    Dept: A14

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES – NORTH DISTRICT

 

 

WAYNE BEUHRING, II,

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

DENNIS DALE PURSLEY, and DOES 1 through 25, inclusive,

 

Defendants. 

  Case Number 25AVCV00263

 

  [TENTATIVE] 

  STATEMENT OF DECISION 

 

 

  Date of Hearing: July 7, 2026

  Dept. A-14 

  Judge William H. Forman 

 

 

      I.          Background

 

This is a personal injury and property case arising from a motor vehicle accident.

 

On February 28, 2025, Plaintiff Wayne Beuhring, II (Plaintiff) filed his form complaint against Defendant Dennis Dale Pursley (Defendant) and DOES 1 through 25, asserting causes of action for personal injury and property damage arising from a motor vehicle accident and general negligence. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Defendant was the operator and owner of a 2022 Chevrolet Silverado 2500, and that on or about March 3, 2023, Defendant’s vehicle failed to stop at a red light and collided with the rear of Plaintiff’s vehicle, causing Plaintiff to sustain serious injuries. (Compl., Cause of Action – General Negligence Attachment.) The Cause of Action – Motor Vehicle Attachment to the Complaint lists the date of the acts as March 8, 2023.

 

On April 7, 2025, Defendant filed his answer.

 

On June 20, 2025, Plaintiff filed an addendum to the complaint, stating the correct date of the automobile collision giving rise to the action is March 3, 2023. This filing was denied as an answer had been filed and the addendum was procedurally improper.

 

On October 23, 2025, Plaintiff moved for leave to file a first amended complaint to name additional defendants in the case. On January 13, 2026, the Court denied Plaintiff’s motion for improperly attempting to reverse pierce the corporate veil.

 

On March 20, 2026, Plaintiff filed his motion for leave to file a first amended complaint.

 

On June 29, 2026, Plaintiff filed a supplemental declaration in support of his motion for leave.

 

No opposition has been filed.

 

-----

 

   II.          Preliminary Procedural Issues

 

Timeliness of Plaintiff’s Supplemental Declaration – Generally, all declarations in support of any petition, motion, or application must be served and submitted at least nine court days before any hearing on the matter at issue. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.513.)

 

Here, Plaintiff filed his supplemental declaration on June 29, 2026, only 5 court days before the hearing on the request. Thus, Plaintiff’s supplemental declaration is not timely.

 

However, in the absence of any facts indicating prejudice to Defendant, the Court will consider the supplemental declaration.

 

 III.          Legal Standard

Standard for Leave to Amend a Complaint – Code of Civil Procedure section 473, subdivision (a)(1) provides, in relevant part: “The court may, in furtherance of justice, and on any terms as may be proper, allow a party to amend any pleading or proceeding by adding or striking out the name of any party, or by correcting a mistake in the name of a party, or a mistake in any other respect; and may, upon like terms, enlarge the time for answer or demurrer. The court may likewise, in its discretion, after notice to the adverse party, allow, upon any terms as may be just, an amendment to any pleading or proceeding in other particulars; and may upon like terms allow an answer to be made after the time limited by this code.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 473, subd. (a)(1).) This discretion should be exercised liberally in favor of amendments, for “judicial policy favors resolution of all disputed matters in the same lawsuit.” (Kittredge Sports Co. v. Superior Court (1989) 213 Cal.App.3d 1045, 1047.)

“The trial court has discretion to permit or deny the amendment of the complaint, but instances justifying the court's denial of leave to amend are rare.” (Armenta ex rel. City of Burbank v. Mueller Co.¿(2006) 142¿Cal.App.4th¿636, 642.)¿ However, “[a]lthough courts are bound to apply a policy of great liberality in permitting amendments to the complaint at any stage of the proceedings, up to and including trial [Citations], this policy should be applied only ‘[w]here no prejudice is shown to the adverse party . . .’ [Citation.] A different result is indicated ‘[w]here¿inexcusable delay and probable prejudice to the opposing party’ is shown. [Citation.]” (Magpali¿v. Farmers Group, Inc.¿(1996) 48¿Cal.App.4th¿471, 487.)

Under rule 3.1324, subdivision (a) of the California Rules of Court, a motion to amend a pleading shall (1) include a copy of the proposed amendment or amended pleading, which must be serially numbered to differentiate it from previous pleadings or amendments; (2) state what allegations in the previous pleading are proposed to be deleted, if any, and where, by page, paragraph and line number, the deleted allegations are located; and (3) state what allegations are proposed to be added to the previous pleading, if any, and where, by page, paragraph, and line number, the additional allegations are located. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1324(a).)

Under subdivision (b), a separate declaration must accompany the motion and must specify (1) the effect of the amendment; (2) why the amendment is necessary and proper; (3) when the facts giving rise to the amended allegations were discovered; and (4) the reasons why the request for amendment was not made earlier. (Id., subd. (b).)

 

-----

 

 IV.          Discussion

 

Application – Plaintiff requests leave to amend to correct an inconsistency in the operative complaint, which presently identifies the date of the underlying motor vehicle accident as both March 3, 2023 and March 8, 2023. (Compl., Cause of Action – General Negligence Attachment; Cause of Action – Motor Vehicle Attachment; Beuhring Decl., ¶ 5.) Plaintiff states that the date of the accident is March 3, 2023, as identified in portions of the complaint and as identified in Defendant’s responses to Form Interrogatories, which were mailed in November of 2025. (Beuhring Decl., ¶ 6.)

 

a.     Procedural Compliance With Rule 3.1324(a)

 

Plaintiff has complied with California Rules of Court rule 3.1324, subdivision (a). Plaintiff filed, concurrently with his request for leave to amend, an ‘Exhibit Index,’ attached to which is a proposed amended complaint which is serially numbered as amended number one. (Index, Ex. 1.)  Plaintiff has also sufficiently stated the allegations to be deleted, being the date of March 8, 2026 on the original Cause of Action – Motor Vehicle Attachment to the complaint. (Beuhring Decl., ¶ 5.) Plaintiff sufficiently states the allegations to be added to the amended complaint, being that the date of the accident is March 3, 2023.

 

Plaintiff’s request is also in compliance with California Rules of Court rule 3.1324, subdivision (b). On June 29, 2026, five court days before the hearing on his request, Plaintiff filed his supplemental declaration to clarify the facts as required by rule 3.1324(b). Plaintiff states with sufficient clarity the effect of the amendment, why the amendment is necessary and proper, the date and manner in which Plaintiff discovered the facts giving rise to the amended allegations, and the reason why Plaintiff did not file his request earlier.

 

Accordingly, Plaintiff’s request is procedurally proper.

 

b.     Leave to Amend

 

The Court finds there is good cause to grant Plaintiff leave to file a first amended complaint. The amendment is limited in scope and accurately reflects the date of the accident as asserted by both Plaintiff and Defendant. Plaintiff seeks a narrow amendment to clarify a date, which has a five-day discrepancy, and does not seek to add any new cause of action, defendants, claims, allegations, injuries, theory of liability, or damages. Plaintiff states he became aware of the risk of uncertainty and confusion arising from the discrepancy following his receipt of insurance policy documentation from Defense counsel on or about February 4, 2026, after which he requested clarification from Defense counsel without response. (Suppl. Dec., ¶¶ 8-9, 16.) The Court also notes that Plaintiff promptly filed a request for amendment on March 20, 2026, which although denied on procedural grounds, indicates a prompt attempt to resolve the matter.

 

Additionally, Defendant has previously indicated in his filings that the appropriate date of the motor vehicle accident is March 3, 2023. (See Defendant’s Opposition to Motion to Compel Disclosure, dated February 5, 2026, p. 1:23-26.) Plaintiff also states that Defendant identified the date of the accident as March 3, 2023, in his discovery responses. (Suppl. Decl., ¶ 7.)

 

The Court notes that on the original form complaint, “General Negligence” was not marked as a cause of action, whereas the box is marked on the proposed first amended complaint. (Compl., p. 3, ¶ 10; PFAC, p. 3, ¶ 10.) However, the Court also notes that the original complaint included a Cause of Action – General Negligence attachment to the complaint, indicating Plaintiff’s assertion of general negligence as a cause of action.

 

Based on the foregoing facts and that March 3, 2023, was identified as the proper date of the accident in the underlying operative complaint, the Court finds that this limited amendment will not prejudice or cause surprise to Defendant.

 

Accordingly, Plaintiff’s request for leave to amend is GRANTED.

 

-----

 

    V.          Conclusion

 

Plaintiff Wayne Beuhring, II’s Motion for Leave to File First Amended is GRANTED. Plaintiff to file the proposed first amended complaint within ten days of this Order.

 


Case Number: 25AVCV00268    Hearing Date: July 7, 2026    Dept: A14

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES – NORTH DISTRICT

 

SHAHIDAH JOHNSON AND CHARLES JOHNSON,

 

                        Plaintiffs,

            v.

 

GENERAL MOTORS, LLC; and DOES 1 through 10, inclusive,

 

                        Defendant.

  Case Number 25AVCV00268

 

  [TENTATIVE]

  STATEMENT OF DECISION

 

 

  Date of Hearing:

  July 7, 2026

  Dept. A-14

  Judge William H. Forman

 

 

      I.          Background

 

The instant Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act (“Song Beverly”) case arises from alleged nonconformities and defects to warranty in Plaintiffs Shahidah and Charles Johnson’s 2017 Chevrolet Malibu, VIN 1G1ZE5ST1HF201713 (hereafter "Vehicle"), which was manufactured and/or distributed by Defendant General Motors, LLC (“GM”). The vehicle was purchased at Antelope Valley Chevrolet in Lancaster, CA, an authorized dealer.

 

On February 28, 2025, Plaintiffs filed their initial complaint.

 

On January 12, 2026, Plaintiffs filed their Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”) against GM and Does 1 through 10, alleging five causes of action: (1) violation of Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (D); (2) violation of Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (B); (3) violation of Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivision (A)(3); (4) breach of the implied warranty of merchantability; (5) fraudulent concealment. 

 

In the SAC, Plaintiffs allege that they entered into a warranty contract with GM on July 4, 2017, regarding their vehicle. (SAC ¶ 6.) Plaintiffs allege that during the express warranty period, the vehicle suffered from engine defects, transmission defects, electrical defects, and a host of other defects and nonconformities. (SAC ¶ 11.) On June 22, 2018, Plaintiffs took the vehicle to an authorized repair facility with complaints about a failure to start – the technician performed warranty repairs and at pick up Plaintiffs were told that the vehicle had been repaired and was working as intended. (SAC ¶ 23.) On March 1, 2018, Plaintiffs once again took the vehicle in for the check engine light, and once again a technician performed warranty repairs and Plaintiffs were told that the vehicle was repaired and working as designed. (SAC ¶ 24.) On June 21, 2022, Plaintiffs took the vehicle in for reduced power and check engine light issue, during which time the technician recommended replacement of the engine due to failure of critical parts. (SAC ¶ 25.) Allegedly tt was at this time that Plaintiffs allegedly learned of GM’s wrongful conduct. (SAC ¶ 26.)

 

 

 

On February 10, 2026, GM filed its Demurrer to the SAC as to the first, second, and third causes of action on the grounds of being barred by the relevant statutes of limitations and statute of repose.

 

On June 29, 2026, Plaintiffs untimely filed an opposition.[1] The opposition was due no later than June 23, 2026.

 

On June 30, 2026, GM filed a reply.

 

   II.          Analysis

 

Standard for Demurrer –The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.30, subd. (a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.)  Concerning the legal sufficiency of a pleading, the sole issue on demurrer is whether the facts pleaded, if true, state a valid cause of action – i.e., if the complaint pleaded facts that would entitle the plaintiff to relief.  (LiMandri v. Judkins (1997) 52 Cal.App.4th 326, 339.)

 

 

-----

 

Meet and Confer – On review of the moving papers, the Court finds that GM satisfied the meet and confer requirements pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 430.41 to bring the instant demurrer.  (Kristen Allison Decl., ¶ 2.) Accordingly, the Court turns to the merits.

-----

 

First, Second, and Third Causes of Action (Violation of Civil Code section 1793.2, subdivisions (D), (B), and (A)(3)) –

 

GM contends, and Plaintiffs do not dispute, that the first, second, and third causes of action are subject to the statutes of limitation and repose set forth in Code of Civil Procedure section 871.20. An action covered by Section 871.20 shall be brought “within one year after the expiration of the applicable express warranty.,” and “[n]otwithstanding subdivision (a), …shall not be brought later than six years after the date of original delivery of the motor vehicle.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 871.21, subdivisions (a)-(b).)

 

GM contends that since Plaintiffs filed the initial complaint on February 28, 2025, and Plaintiffs entered into the warranty contract for the vehicle on July 4, 2017 (presumably the delivery date), then the six-year statute of repose period ended on July 3, 2023. (Mot., at p. 5.) As to the statute of limitations, pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21, subdivision (a), because the express warranties for the bumper to bumper and the powertrain expired on July 3, 2020 & July 3, 2022, then the statute of limitations ran, at the latest on July 3,2023, Plaintiffs original complaint filed on February 28, 2025 was past the July 3, 2023 end date of both the statute of limitations and statute of repose.  (Id.)

 

Plaintiffs do not contest this timeline. Rather, they argue that 1) AB 1755 was enacted in September 2024 and only became effective on January 1, 2025, and therefore should not apply retroactively to claims that accrued years, and 2) in any event, Plaintiffs have pled facts sufficient for equitable tolling of the subject claims.

 

As the Court determined in its order on the previous demurrer, Section 871.21 is to be applied retroactively.

 

 

 

As to the tolling allegations, GM argues that the SAC fails to allege any facts establishing that the first and third tolling circumstances under Code of Civil Procedure, section 871.21, subdivision (c), are satisfied. (Id.) For the second tolling provision, GM argues that the SAC only alleges that the vehicle was out of service for three days and thus the claims may be tolled a maximum of three days, which is not enough to overcome the deficit. (Mot., at pgs. 5-6.) In reference to the SAC’s allegations to class action, discovery rule, repair doctrine, and estoppel tolling, GM maintains the argument that the Legislature did not expressly apply these rules and doctrines to the statute of repose here, and in any case, the SAC fails to sufficiently plead facts establishing that the statute would be tolled under these doctrines. (Mot., at pg. 6.)

 

Lastly, GM argues that if Plaintiffs should argue in opposition that the statute of limitations and statutes of repose do not apply to the because it would be a “retroactive” application, GM points to this Court’s prior demurrer ruling as to the FAC, and argues that since the opt-in provision did not go into effect until April 1, 2025, GM could not have been required to opt-in. (Id.)

 

In opposition, as to equitable tolling, Plaintiffs argue that they have cured the defects noted in the Court’s prior order to allege that Plaintiffs only became aware of GM’s breach after multiple repair attempts. (Opp., at pg. 2.) As to the statute of limitations argument, Plaintiffs contend that the new limitations period cannot be retroactively applied to run pre-effective date. (Id.) AB 1755 was enacted in September 2024 and became effective four months later. Plaintiffs argue that since courts have previously held that eight months is a reasonable time after a statutory filing period change, their complaint was filed within a reasonable time after the passage of the new law. (Id.)

 

As the Court noted in its previous Order on December 9, 2025, Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21 became effective on January 1, 2025, rendering it operative at the time Plaintiffs filed their original complaint on February 28, 2025. The cases Plaintiffs cite to in support of their retroactive argument are either not binding on this Court due to being unpublished or do not pertain to Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21. (Opp., at p. 2.) Code of Civil Procedure section 871.30, subdivision (a) states:

 

“Within 30 days of the effective date of the act adding this section [i.e., by May 1, 2025], a manufacturer may elect to be governed by this chapter for all actions described in subdivision (a) of Section 871.20 with respect to all of its motor vehicles sold in the year 2025 and in all prior years by providing written notice of that election to the Arbitration Certification Program within the Department of Consumer Affairs.”

 

(Emphasis added.) GM opted into the new lemon law procedures on April 23, 2025. (California Dept. of Consumer Affairs, Arbitration Certification Program Website.) Plaintiffs do not allege in their Complaint, or argue in their Opposition, that GM did not opt in to Section 871.21. As the statue expressly applies to sales of motor vehicles in years prior to 2025, the legislature provided that the statue would apply retroactively.

 

Plaintiffs argue that it would be unfair and a deprivation of their rights to due process to apply a statue retroactively so as to “wipe out an accrued cause of action that is not barred by the then applicable statute of limitations.” (Opposition, at 2.) But the enactment of AB1755 was not a surprise. Plaintiffs had from September 2024 to January 1, 2025 to file their claim as to a vehicle they purchased over seven years before. Plaintiffs admit that “hundreds and hundreds of people” did just that. (Opposition, at 3.)

 

Given the retroactive application of the statue, the only question is whether there is some reason the statues of repose and limitations do not bar Plaintiffs’ claims

 

Plaintiffs argue that, notwithstanding the statutes of repose and limitations, their claims are subject to equitable tolling. The elements of the equitable tolling rule are: (1) timely notice to defendant; (2) lack of prejudice; and (3) Plaintiff’s reasonable and good faith conduct. (McDonald v. Antelope Valley Community College Dist. (2008) 45 Cal.4th 88, 102.)

 

As to the statue of repose, Plaintiff’s argument is a non-starter. Statutes of repose are generally not subject to equitable tolling. (See MACH-1 RSMH, LLC v. Darras (2024) 103 Cal.App.5th 1288, 1302 [“statutes of repose are generally not subject to tolling”].); Plaintiffs’ cite no authority recognizing equitable tolling of a statute of repose, and the Court is aware of none. Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21, subdivision (b) therefore bars Plaintiffs’ claims regardless of any equitable doctrine Plaintiffs invoke.

 

As to the statute of limitations, the Court finds that Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21, subdivision (c) does not necessarily preclude equitable tolling of the Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21, subdivision (a) statute of limitations under the appropriate circumstances, as the conditions of Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21, subdivision (c) are not exclusive. Plaintiffs allege that GM is estopped from relying on any statutes of limitation because GM fraudulently concealed defects and refused to investigate or remedy said issues. (SAC ¶¶ 41-44.) Plaintiffs’ conclusory statements of fraudulent concealment do not establish the elements for equitable tolling.

 

Accordingly, the Court SUSTAINS the demurrer.

 

[

-----

 

Leave to Amend –

Leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (Goodman v. Kennedy¿(1976), 18 Cal.3d 335, 348.) While under California law leave to amend is liberally granted, “leave to amend should not be granted where, in all probability, amendment would be futile.” (Vaillette v. Fireman's Fund Ins. Co. (1993), 18 Cal. App. 4th 680, 685).¿ “A trial court does not abuse its discretion when it sustains a demurrer without¿leave to amend¿if either (a) the facts and the nature of the claims are clear and no liability exists, or (b) it is probable from the nature of the defects and previous unsuccessful attempts to plead that the plaintiff cannot state a claim.” (Cantu v. Resolution Trust Corp.¿(1992)¿4 Cal.App.4th 857, 889.)¿¿¿

 

The Court SUSTAINS the Demurrer without leave to amend because, regardless of whether Plaintiffs could plead facts sufficient to establish equitable tolling, the six-year statute of repose stands as an insurmountable barrier. The Court also notes that Plaintiffs previously were given leave to plead facts to support equitable tolling, and again have failed to do so.

-----

 

 

 III.          Conclusion

 

Defendant General Motors, LLC’s Demurrer is SUSTAINED without leave to amend.

 


[1] The Court notes that while the opposition was untimely, because GM filed a reply and indicated it “wishes to proceed with[] the Demurrer without delay,” although it disputes opposing counsel’s contention that the untimely filing was due to mistake, the Court considers the opposition on its merits.


Case Number: 25AVCV00396    Hearing Date: July 7, 2026    Dept: A14

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES – NORTH DISTRICT

 

RANDY ROSHAWN YOUNG,

 

                        Plaintiff,

            v.

 

MIRAGE POST ACUTE; WELLSPRINGS POST-ACUTE CENTER; and DOES 1 through 20, inclusive,

 

                        Defendants.

  Case Number 25AVCV00396

 

  [TENTATIVE]

  STATEMENT OF DECISION

 

 

  Date of Hearing:

  July 7, 2026

  Dept. A-14

  Judge William H. Forman

 

 

      I.          Background

 

The instant case arises from alleged personal injuries sustained by Plaintiff Randy Roshawn Young (“Plaintiff”) when he was allegedly attacked at Defendant Mirage Post Acute’s, dba Defendant Wellsprings Post-Acute Center, nursing facility by another patient.

 

On March 26, 2025, Plaintiff filed a Personal Injury Complaint against Defendants Mirage Post Acute, who is doing business as Defendant Wellsprings Post-Acute Center, Angel Lopez, and Does 1 through 20, alleging a single cause of action for general negligence.

 

On April 22, 2025, Plaintiff filed an amendment to the complaint, naming Defendant Geri-Care V, LLC as Doe 1.

 

On July 11 and 17, 2025, a request for dismissal as to Defendants Angel Lopez and Geri-Care V, LLC was entered.

 

On July 16, 2025, Plaintiff’s request for entry of default as to Defendants Mirage Post Acute and Wellsprings Post-Acute Center (collectively, “Mirage”) was entered.

 

On August 8, 2025, a stipulation and order to set aside default judgment pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 473 was granted.

 

On November 20, 2025, Mirage filed an answer.

 

On January 27, March 2, March 12, and April 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed amendments to the complaint, naming Defendants Kenneth Aronson, Kenneth Erenson, the Estate of Kenneth Aronson, and Global Alliance Protection as Does 2-5.

 

On March 9, 2026, the Court granted the Stipulation RE: Confidentiality allowing Mirage to release the personal identification information of the alleged assailant. 

 

On April 8, 2026, Mirage filed the operative Motion to Compel Arbitration.

 

On June 17, 2026, Plaintiff filed an opposition.

 

On June 26, 2026, Mirage filed a reply.  

 

   II.          Analysis

 

Standard for Motion to Compel Arbitration – Under California and federal law, public policy favors arbitration as an efficient and less expensive means of resolving private disputes. (Moncharsh v. Heily & Blasé (1992) 3 Cal.4th 1, 8-9 (Moncharsh); AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion (2011) 563 U.S. 333, 339.) Accordingly, whether an agreement is governed by the California Arbitration Act or the Federal Arbitration Act, courts resolve doubt about an arbitration agreement’s scope in favor of arbitration. (Moncharsh, supra, 3 Cal.4th at p. 9; Comedy Club, Inc. v. Improv West Associates (9th Cir. 2009) 553 F.3d 1277, 1284; see also Engalla v. Permanente Med. Grp., Inc. (1997) 15 Cal.4th 951, 971-72 [“California law incorporates many of the basic policy objectives contained in the Federal Arbitration Act, including a presumption in favor of arbitrability [citation] and a requirement that an arbitration agreement must be enforced on the basis of state law standards that apply to contracts in general [citation].”].) “[U]nder both the FAA and California law, ‘arbitration agreements are valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract.’” (Higgins v. Superior Court (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 1238, 1247.)

 

The party seeking to compel arbitration bears the burden of proving the existence of a valid arbitration agreement by the preponderance of the evidence.  (Engalla, supra, 15 Cal.4th 951, 972.)  A petition to compel arbitration must allege both a “written agreement to arbitrate” the controversy, and that a party to that agreement “refuses to arbitrate” the controversy. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1281.2.) It then becomes plaintiff’s burden, in opposing the motion, to prove by a preponderance of the evidence any fact necessary to her opposition. (Ibid.)

 

“Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.2 requires a trial court to grant a petition to compel arbitration ‘if the court determines that an agreement to arbitrate the controversy exists.’”  (Avery v. Integrated Healthcare Holdings, Inc. (2013) 218 Cal.App.4th 50, 59 (Avery), quoting Code Civ. Proc., § 1281.2).) Accordingly, “when presented with a petition to compel arbitration, the court’s first task is to determine whether the parties have in fact agreed to arbitrate the dispute.” (Id., at p. 59.) Generally, on a petition to compel arbitration, the court must grant the petition unless it finds either (1) no written agreement to arbitrate exists; (2) the right to compel arbitration has been waived; (3) grounds exist for revocation of the agreement; or (4) litigation is pending that may render the arbitration unnecessary or create conflicting rulings on common issues. (Ibid.; see also Condee v. Longwood Management Corp. (2001) 88 Cal.App.4th 215, 218-219.) “In these summary proceedings the trial court sits as a trier of fact, weighing all the affidavits, declarations, and other documentary evidence, as well as oral testimony received at the court’s discretion, to reach a final determination.” (Avery, supra, 218 Cal.App.4th at p. 59; accord Rosenthal v. Great Western Financial Securities Corp. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 394, 413.)

 

 

-----

 

Discussion

 

Existence of an Arbitration Agreement –

Mirage advances the declaration of Isaiah Navarro, the Admissions Assistant at Mirage who has familiarity with the admission process and the documents executed by residents or their representatives upon admission, including the Arbitration Provision in contention, and the facility’s practices/procedures regarding record maintenance. (Navarro Decl., ¶¶ 1-2.) Mr. Navarro also states it is the standard practice of the facility to explain the Arbitration Agreement’s (“Agreement”) terms and conditions to each resident prior to execution, and residents are informed that execution is voluntary and residency is not conditioned upon consent to the Agreement. (Navarro Decl., ¶ 5.) Residents are provided with a 30-day period post-execution to cancel the agreement, but upon Mr. Navarro’s review of Mirage’s records, Plaintiff has not submitted a written notice of cancellation. (Navarro Decl., ¶ 7.) Mr. Navarro states that he “personally met with Plaintiff on October 23, 2024, to review and explain the admissions packet. I separately explained the Arbitration Agreement. I specifically recall meeting the Plaintiff and reviewing these documents with him.” (Navarro Decl., ¶ 10.) Mr. Navarro explains that prior to execution, Plaintiff undertook a Brief Interview for Mental Status assessment to evaluate his cognitive capacity, which was found to be intact. (Navarro Decl., ¶ 11.)

 

Plaintiff does not dispute the existence of an arbitration agreement in opposition.

 

Mirage’s counsel also attests to his submission to opposing counsel of a Formal Arbitration Demand Letter on January 23, 2026, which was unsuccessful. (Williams Decl., ¶¶ 17-18.) Counsel has also attached a copy of said Agreement. (Williams Decl., ¶ 6, Exh. B.)

 

Mirage has carried its threshold burden to show that an arbitration agreement exists between the parties, and Plaintiff has refused to arbitrate his claims.

 

-----

 

FAA applies & Code of Civil Procedure Section 1281.2, subdivision (c) does not bar the Petition –

Plaintiff argues that the Court should deny arbitration under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1281.2, subdivision (c) because the other named Defendants in this action are not signatories to the arbitration agreement and all of Plaintiff’s claims arise from the same transaction. (Opp., at p. 4.) Plaintiff cites to Cronus Investments, Inc. v. Concierge Services (2005) 35 Cal.4th 376, 393 & Avila v. Southern California Specialty Care, Inc. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 835, 844-845, but those cases are distinguishable from the facts here.

 

In Cronus, the Supreme Court explicitly held:

“Our opinion does not preclude parties to an arbitration agreement to expressly designate that any arbitration proceeding should move forward under the FAA's procedural provisions rather than under state procedural law. We simply hold that the language of the arbitration clause in this case, calling for the application of the FAA “if it would be applicable,” should not be read to preclude the application of 1281.2(c), because it does not conflict with the applicable provisions of the FAA and does not undermine or frustrate the FAA's substantive policy favoring arbitration.”

(Cronus, supra, 35 Cal.4th at p. 394.) The Supreme Court did not denounce the express contractual waiver of Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.2, subdivision (c) and the express designation for an arbitration proceeding to move forward under the FAA.
